Solar basics

What happens to solar during a grid outage?

The most common post-blackout surprise: the panels on the roof did nothing. Why that happens, and what it takes to keep the lights on.

Published 16 September 2026Updated 15 October 20266 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

The first blackout after solar installation is when many owners learn something nobody explained clearly: a standard grid-connected system switches itself off within seconds of an outage, even in bright sunshine. It is not a fault. It is, in fact, one of the system's most important safety behaviours.

Why solar alone goes dark

Every grid-connected inverter is required to have anti-islanding protection: if the grid voltage disappears, the inverter shuts down immediately so it cannot energise the network while linesworkers are repairing it. A solar system that kept producing into a blacked-out street would be a lethal hazard to exactly the people trying to restore your power. The shutdown is automatic, mandatory and correct.

What it takes to keep power during an outage

  • A battery system with backup capability, wired to supply a designated set of circuits — the standard residential option.
  • Backup circuits decided during design: usually lights, fridge, internet, a few power points, and any medically essential equipment.
  • Whole-home backup: possible with larger-capacity equipment rated for the whole house's loads — including the starting surge of motors and compressors — but a significant step up in battery power and cost.
  • Generators remain an option, but must be connected through a proper changeover arrangement by a licensed electrician — never improvised with extension cords and back-feeding.

How backup circuits are chosen

  1. List what genuinely needs to run: fridge and freezer, internet and phone charging, lighting, a heating or cooling device for extreme weather, medical equipment if relevant.
  2. Note the starting surge of anything with a motor or compressor — it can be several times the running draw.
  3. Compare the list against the battery's continuous and peak power ratings, not just its stored energy.
  4. Decide the run time you want — a few hours of essentials or an overnight — and check it against usable capacity.

What a home backup actually delivers

A typical well-designed essentials circuit can run lighting, refrigeration, communications and small appliances for many hours on a modest home battery. What it cannot do is treat the battery like a generator: during a long outage, recharge comes only from solar, and solar recharge depends on the weather. In a multi-day cloudy outage, a battery that started full will end empty unless loads are managed.

A battery in an outage is a rationed resource, not a power station

Plan for the realistic case: several hours to a day of essentials, managed deliberately. If prolonged, whole-home outage coverage is a genuine requirement, the conversation belongs in design — with honest numbers for what it costs and what it can run.

Testing and expectations

  • Ask for a backup test as part of commissioning: how the changeover behaves, which circuits stay live, and how to read the battery's remaining charge.
  • Know the reserve setting: most systems hold a minimum state of charge for backup — confirm it is configured for your priorities.
  • Check monitoring access during an outage: some systems report through the home network, which may itself be offline; know how to read the battery's local display as a fallback.
  • Revisit the arrangement if circumstances change — medical equipment, remote work, or elderly household members can shift what 'essentials' must include.

Key takeaways

  • Standard solar shuts down in a blackout by law, to keep the network safe for repairs.
  • Outage power requires a battery with backup wiring — decided at design time, not after.
  • Backup circuits are a chosen list of essentials, sized against the battery's kW and kWh ratings.
  • Long outages drain the battery faster than the sun refills it in poor weather — manage loads deliberately.
  • Commissioning should include a walkthrough of how the backup actually behaves.
